back: The process by which the primary sex organs produce gametes - sperms in the testis and ovum in the ovary.
The pouch outside the abdominal cavity that holds the testes and keeps them 2-2.5 degrees C below internal body temperature, which is necessary for spermatogenesis.
About 250 compartments in each testis; each contains one to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules.
Cells lining the seminiferous tubule that provide nutrition to the developing germ cells.
Interstitial cells outside the seminiferous tubules that synthesise and secrete androgens.
Secretions of the seminal vesicles, prostate and bulbourethral glands; rich in fructose, calcium and certain enzymes. With sperms it forms semen.
The funnel-shaped part of the oviduct closer to the ovary; its edges carry fimbriae that collect the ovum after ovulation.
The inner glandular layer of the uterus lining the uterine cavity; it undergoes cyclical changes during the menstrual cycle.
The middle, thick smooth-muscle layer of the uterus; it shows strong contraction during delivery of the baby.
The transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa (sperms).
The release of sperms from the seminiferous tubules, after their heads become embedded in the Sertoli cells.
The cap-like structure covering the anterior portion of the sperm head, filled with enzymes that help fertilisation of the ovum.
The process of formation of a mature female gamete; it begins in the fetal ovary and no new oogonia are added after birth.
The mature ovarian follicle that ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovum) during ovulation.
Menarche is the first menstruation at puberty; menopause is the cessation of menstrual cycles around 50 years of age.
The rapid mid-cycle rise of luteinising hormone that ruptures the Graafian follicle and causes ovulation.
The remaining part of the Graafian follicle after ovulation; it secretes large amounts of progesterone that maintain the endometrium.
The fusion of a sperm with an ovum, normally in the ampullary region of the fallopian tube, forming a diploid zygote.
The embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres formed by cleavage as the zygote moves through the isthmus towards the uterus.
The stage after the morula, with an outer trophoblast and an inner cell mass; the trophoblast attaches to the endometrium.
The embedding of the blastocyst in the endometrium of the uterus after the trophoblast attaches and uterine cells cover it; it leads to pregnancy.
The structural and functional unit formed by chorionic villi interdigitated with uterine tissue, between the foetus and the mother.
Human chorionic gonadotropin and human placental lactogen - hormones produced by the placenta in women only during pregnancy.
A hormone secreted by the ovary in the later phase of pregnancy.
The average duration of human pregnancy, about 9 months.
The process of delivery of the foetus (childbirth), caused by vigorous contraction of the uterus at the end of pregnancy.
Mild uterine contractions induced by signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta; it triggers release of oxytocin from the maternal pituitary.
The milk produced during the initial few days of lactation; it contains antibodies essential for developing resistance in the new-born.
A membrane that often covers the vaginal opening partially; its presence or absence is not a reliable indicator of virginity or sexual experience.
Clusters of cells inside each mammary lobe that secrete milk, which is stored in their lumens.
